findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that each worker gets its own one-way `Pipe(duplex=False)` (one per Process), with the parent holding each read end.
evidence: 'Each runs `_commit_worker`, which sends ("ok", atomic_close) or ("error", repr) back over a one-way `Pipe`'
findings.finding: The Pipe topology is ambiguous. The plan says 'a one-way `Pipe`' (singular) for 2 Processes. It does not say whether each worker gets its own Pipe or both share one. A shared multiprocessing Connection is not safe for two concurrent writers.
findings.location: Approach — 'sends ... back over a one-way `Pipe`; the parent receives both outcomes'
scenarios: The executor puts both workers on one Pipe, and the two concurrent sends interleave or corrupt each other.
findings.suggested_fix: Create one `ctx.Pipe(duplex=False)` per worker and pass only the send end to that worker's Process.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Require a try/finally that terminates any still-alive worker and joins all workers, so no process outlives the test on any path.

findings.finding: There is no cleanup path on failure. ProcessPoolExecutor's context manager shut workers down automatically. The plan's bare Processes have no stated try/finally to terminate and join them if `recv` raises or an assertion fails before join.
findings.location: Approach — replacement of ProcessPoolExecutor with 2 plain `Process`es
scenarios: An assertion fails between `recv()` and `join()`, leaving orphan spawn processes that keep publishing to the bundle path during later tests.
findings.suggested_fix: `finally: for p in procs: if p.is_alive(): p.terminate(); p.join(timeout=...)`

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State explicitly that `_commit_worker` is changed (or wrapped by a new module-level, picklable entry point) to take the Pipe's send end and send `("ok", atomic_close)` or `("error", repr(exc))`, then close it, because today it only returns a dict.

findings.finding: The plan says each worker 'runs `_commit_worker`, which sends `("ok", atomic_close)` or `("error", repr)` back over a one-way `Pipe`'. Read as a description of existing code, this is wrong. Today `_commit_worker(repo, ticket, result)` returns `dict(_commit_bundle(...).atomic_close)`; it takes no connection and sends nothing. findings.location: Approach — 'Each runs `_commit_worker`, which sends ("ok", atomic_close) or ("error", repr) back over a one-way `Pipe`'

findings.suggested_fix: Change the Approach sentence to say that `_commit_worker` gains a `conn` parameter (the Pipe's send end). It wraps the existing `dict(_commit_bundle(...).atomic_close)` call in try/except, sends `("ok", outcome)` or `("error", repr(exc))`, and closes `conn` in a `finally` block.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say how the parent detects a dead worker: close the parent's write ends after `start()`, treat EOFError/a nonzero `exitcode` as a test failure that names the worker, and terminate and join both children in a `finally`. Also decide whether the 203-247 s measured runtime needs an explicit `@pytest.mark.timeout(N)` with a comment, as pyproject.toml prescribes.
evidence: Plan: 'the parent receives both outcomes and joins the workers' — nothing on EOF handling, exitcode, or cleanup on failure
pyproject.toml:750-753: 'because `timeout_method = "thread"` expires a test with `os._exit(1)` ... it kills the whole xdist worker (`node down: Not properly terminated`)'
pyproject.toml:761-765: a test that legitimately runs longer should override with `@pytest.mark.timeout(N)` and a comment saying why
Ticket sweltering-difficult-drongo: the test took 247 s and 203 s on a loaded host; the plan's own after-run took 208.76 s, so it already runs near the 300 s budget
findings.finding: Replacing ProcessPoolExecutor with plain Processes and a Pipe removes the existing protection against a worker dying, and the plan does not replace it. ProcessPoolExecutor raises BrokenProcessPool when a worker dies. With plain Process plus Pipe, a child that dies before sending (an import failure under spawn, a segfault, an os._exit, or an exception outside the try that sends `("error", repr)`) leaves the parent blocked forever in `recv()`, unless the parent has closed its own copies of the write ends so it gets EOFError. The plan does not say to close them, check `exitcode` after `join`, or terminate and join the children in a `finally`. Its only backstop is the 300 s suite budget. pyproject.toml documents that this budget uses `timeout_method = "thread"`, which calls `os._exit(1)` and kills the whole xdist worker ("node down: Not properly terminated"), leaving the non-daemon children orphaned. That is the crash mode the budget's comments warn about, not a clean failure.
findings.location: Approach — 'Each runs `_commit_worker`, which sends ... over a one-way `Pipe`; the parent receives both outcomes and joins the workers ... the suite's 300 s per-test budget bounds a hang.'
scenarios: A spawned worker fails to import rebar or crashes before sending: the parent blocks in recv() until the thread-method timeout runs os._exit(1), the xdist worker dies, and the actual cause is never reported.
On a host under load ~45, the legitimate run exceeds 300 s: the xdist worker crashes instead of the test reporting a failure, and the child processes leak.
One worker raises: the parent gets ('error', repr) but the plan does not say whether the other child is still joined or terminated before the assertion fails.
findings.suggested_fix: Use one `Pipe(duplex=False)` per worker. After `p.start()`, call `send_conn.close()` in the parent. For each worker, call `recv_conn.recv()`; EOFError becomes `pytest.fail(f"worker {i} exited without reporting (exitcode={p.exitcode})")`. Then `p.join()` and assert `p.exitcode == 0`. Wrap everything in try/finally that calls `p.terminate()` and `p.join()` on any child still alive.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the parent closes its copy of each send end after `start()`, treats EOFError as a worker failure, and asserts each worker's exitcode is 0 after join.
evidence: The removed `future.result(timeout=60)` used to surface worker death or hangs; nothing in the plan replaces it.
The plan does not mention closing the parent's copy of the send end, nor `poll(timeout)` or exitcode checks.
findings.finding: The plan does not say how the parent detects a worker that crashes before sending. If the parent keeps the child's send end open, `recv()` never raises EOFError. The test then hangs until the suite timeout, and no diagnostic says which worker died.
findings.location: Approach — 'the parent receives both outcomes and joins the workers'
scenarios: A worker segfaults or is killed by the sandbox. The parent blocks on `recv()` until the 300 s per-test kill, and the failure gives no cause.
findings.suggested_fix: After `p.start()`, call `send_conn.close()` in the parent. Wrap `recv()` to turn EOFError into a failure message naming the worker and its exitcode, then assert `p.exitcode == 0` after `join()`.

findings.finding: The rewrite changes how a crashed worker shows up, and the plan does not acknowledge this. ProcessPoolExecutor raised BrokenProcessPool promptly when a worker died. With plain Process plus a single one-way Pipe, a worker that dies before sending will block the parent's `recv()`, unless the parent closes its copy of the send end after starting both workers. If it does not, the failure appears only when the 300 s per-test budget expires, with no diagnostic. The plan's justification covers hangs only ('the suite's 300 s per-test budget bounds a hang'), not crashes. The measured passing run already used 208.76 s of that 300 s budget.
findings.location: Approach — 'sends ("ok", atomic_close) or ("error", repr) back over a one-way Pipe; the parent receives both outcomes and joins the workers'
scenarios: A worker segfaults or is OOM-killed during the commit. The parent blocks in `recv()` and the test dies at the 300 s suite budget, instead of failing fast with the worker's exitcode.
A worker raises before reaching its try/except send path. No outcome is sent, and the failure looks like a hang rather than a crash.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach, add: 'After starting both Processes the parent closes its copy of the Pipe send end, so `recv()` raises EOFError if a worker exits without sending; after `join()` the test asserts each worker's exitcode is 0 and fails with that exitcode otherwise.' This keeps the drongo decision (no wall-clock bound) while making crashes fail fast.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the Pipe protocol: the parent closes each child's send end right after Process.start(), treats EOFError from recv() as a failed worker (and reports its exitcode), and _commit_worker's new signature takes a Connection and send()s the tagged outcome.
evidence: tests/interfaces/lifecycle/test_atomic_completion_close.py:120-122: `def _commit_worker(repo: str, ticket: str, result: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, object]: ... return dict(_commit_bundle(...).atomic_close)`. It returns a value and sends nothing.
pyproject.toml:766 `timeout = 300`; docs/local-dev-env.md:626 says timeout_method = "thread", so a hang ends in the guard's stack-dump exit, not a normal test failure.
Plan Testing: "1 passed in 208.76 s, load average ~30". The happy path already uses about 70% of the guard budget.
Evidence class: Partially-verified. The happy path is measured; the behaviour when a worker dies before sending is not described or measured.
findings.finding: The plan says each worker "sends ("ok", atomic_close) or ("error", repr) back over a one-way Pipe; the parent receives both outcomes and joins the workers". It does not say that the parent closes its copy of each child's send end after start(). With multiprocessing.Pipe(duplex=False), the parent's recv() raises EOFError when a child dies before sending (spawn bootstrap/import failure, OOM kill, signal) only if every write end is closed. Otherwise recv() blocks until the 300 s thread-method hang guard fires. The plan treats a hang as bounded by that guard, but under the observed load the passing run already took 208.76 s, so a wedged recv turns a clear child crash into an opaque timeout. The plan also does not say that _commit_worker changes from its current `(repo, ticket, result) -> dict` signature to one that takes a Connection and calls send().
findings.location: Approach — "replace the ProcessPoolExecutor with 2 plain multiprocessing spawn-context Processes ... over a one-way Pipe; the parent receives both outcomes and joins the workers"
scenarios: A spawn child fails while re-importing the test module (or is OOM-killed) before calling send(). The parent still holds the write end, so recv() blocks and the thread-method timeout dumps stacks after 300 s instead of reporting the child's exit code.
Under sandbox load, a slow but healthy run plus any setup overhead gets close to 300 s and is hard to tell apart from a real hang.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach, state: `recv_conn, send_conn = ctx.Pipe(duplex=False); p = ctx.Process(target=_commit_worker, args=(repo, ticket, result, send_conn)); p.start(); send_conn.close()`. Then in the parent, wrap `recv_conn.recv()` and on EOFError fail with `p.exitcode`. Optionally call `recv_conn.poll(timeout)` before recv so a dead child is caught well before the 300 s guard.

findings.finding: The plan keeps the marker because '`Pipe`/`Process` still need it on hosts without POSIX semaphores'. Nothing backs this, and it is likely false for the planned design. A spawn-context `Pipe(duplex=False)` is built on `os.pipe()`, and `Process.start()` under spawn does not create a SemLock. The SemLock dependency in the current test comes from ProcessPoolExecutor's internal queues and locks, which the rewrite removes. Unless `_commit_bundle` or the rewritten worker creates a multiprocessing synchronization primitive, the marker would no longer describe what the test needs.
findings.location: Approach — 'The `requires_posix_named_semaphore` marker stays, since `Pipe`/`Process` still need it on hosts without POSIX semaphores.'
scenarios: On a host where SemLock creation is denied but fork/exec and os.pipe work, the rewritten test is still skipped as a counted sandbox-compatibility skip even though it could run, which hides coverage of the publication race.

It says the marker stays 'since `Pipe`/`Process` still need it on hosts without POSIX semaphores'. But `multiprocessing.Pipe(duplex=False)` is backed by `os.pipe()`, and a spawn-context `Process` creates no SemLock. After the rewrite the test uses no POSIX named semaphore. The plan gives no measurement or citation showing that Pipe or spawn Process needs a POSIX named semaphore. Evidence class: Unverified, and likely Contradicted by CPython's multiprocessing.connection.Pipe and popen_spawn_posix implementations.
findings.finding: The plan justifies keeping the marker with "The requires_posix_named_semaphore marker stays, since Pipe/Process still need it on hosts without POSIX semaphores." That capability claim is not verified, and CPython's implementation appears to contradict it. multiprocessing.Pipe is built on os.pipe() (duplex=False) or socket.socketpair() (duplex=True), and a spawn-context Process.start() does not construct a _multiprocessing.SemLock. The probe the marker gates on checks only SemLock construction (_sandbox_capabilities.py:194-198). After the rewrite the test may need nothing that the marker checks. The marker would then skip a test that could run, and the rationale recorded in the plan would be wrong.
findings.location: Approach — "The requires_posix_named_semaphore marker stays, since Pipe/Process still need it on hosts without POSIX semaphores."
scenarios: On a host without POSIX named semaphores but with working os.pipe and spawn, the rewritten test is skipped (counted) even though it would run, which quietly reduces coverage of the same-ticket race.
A later maintainer trusts the recorded rationale and adds the marker to other Pipe/Process-only tests.
